q: What is the difference between a champion and a coach in sales?
a: A coach gives you information and advice about the buying organisation but will not spend their own credibility on your behalf. A champion has power and influence, has a personal stake in your success, and actively sells your solution internally. The simplest test is action: ask a contact to arrange a meeting with the economic buyer or to put their name to a recommendation. A coach hesitates. A champion does it.

q: Can the economic buyer be the champion?
a: Yes, but it is uncommon in larger enterprise deals. The economic buyer controls the budget and is usually weighing your project against several others competing for the same money, so they tend to stay neutral. A champion more often sits one or two levels below, owns the problem directly, and builds the case that the economic buyer then approves. If the economic buyer is genuinely championing you, still find a second strong relationship.

q: How many champions should you have in an enterprise deal?
a: Aim for one clear champion who leads the internal case, supported by two or three other strong relationships in the account. A single champion is a single point of failure: if they change role, leave or lose influence, the deal can stall overnight. Additional relationships across finance, IT or the user team make the deal more resilient and give your champion allies in internal meetings.

q: How early in a deal should you identify a champion?
a: Start looking in the first discovery conversations and aim to have a tested champion before the deal reaches a formal evaluation or proposal stage. Early on you are looking for candidates: people who own the problem and gain from solving it. By the time you are discussing commercial terms, you should have seen that person take real action for you, such as securing access to the economic buyer.
